subtopicTitle: Bi-elliptic transfer — when it wins over Hohmann

cards.back: A three-impulse maneuver using two elliptical arcs: first burn raises apogee to an intermediate radius $r_2 \gg r_3$, second burn at apogee raises perigee to final radius $r_3$, third burn circularizes at $r_3$.

cards.front: How many impulses does a Hohmann transfer require versus a bi-elliptic transfer?
State the approximate radius-ratio threshold above which a bi-elliptic transfer can require less total $\Delta v$ than a Hohmann transfer.
Write the total $\Delta v$ expression for a Hohmann transfer from circular orbit $r_1$ to $r_3$.
Write the total $\Delta v$ expression for a bi-elliptic transfer with intermediate apogee $r_2$.
Why can a bi-elliptic transfer ever beat Hohmann despite an extra burn?
cards.back: At very large $r_2$ the first and second burns become nearly tangential to escape; the velocity increments needed at high altitude are tiny, so the sum of three small burns can be less than the two large plane-change-free burns of Hohmann when $r_3/r_1$ is large.

Bi-elliptic $\Delta v$ approaches the sum of escape from $r_1$ plus capture from infinity into $r_3$; this limit is always worse than a finite optimal $r_2$ but still illustrates the asymptotic advantage for huge radius ratios.

cards.front: For a given $r_3/r_1>11.94$, how should $r_2$ be chosen to minimize bi-elliptic $\Delta v$?
cards.back: Solve $\partial\Delta v_{BE}/\partial r_2=0$ numerically; the optimum lies at finite but large $r_2$ (typically hundreds to thousands of $r_3$).
